name: Freya Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the grid-connection crew at Ostwind Energy. We build the lines that carry power from new solar and wind farms across the farmland to the nearest substation, so I spend my days in fields with a lot of sky. Concrete foundations, steel poles, stringing the wire, a lot of waiting for the crane. I'm 58 and a second-year apprentice. For thirty years before that I rigged lights for concerts and theatres, freelance, until the shows stopped during the pandemic and never really came back for me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Heights don't bother me at all, after decades hanging off theatre grids, so that's the one thing I'm ahead on. What wears me out is the heavy hauling and the rule books. The young men pull cable like it's nothing and I'm puffing, and the safety codes are thick as a phone book. I use AI every day to quiz myself on the codes and to sort my photos of faulty fittings, and Rashid, my crew lead, teases me that I'll end up with a robot for a husband. My husband Jonas is a carpenter, so he's not worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. I'll take you through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, the robots aren't coming, let's get on with it. Maybe I'd post something a bit cheeky about all the money people spent on hype. I wouldn't make a big deal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little disappointed. I like gadgets, and I'd been half hoping the job would get easier on my shoulders. But it means steady work until I'm 66, and that's not a bad deal for someone who spent thirty years never knowing next month's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, qualify in 2027, and keep using the AI tools I already use. I'd probably buy a better tablet for studying. Otherwise nothing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with a tiny sigh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never knew next month's pay. What did that teach you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To keep a jar. Jonas and I always have a few months put by, about four right now. Freelancing taught us that the phone can stop ringing on a Tuesday. It also taught me not to panic when it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would even small AI changes reach your crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They already have, a bit. The planning team uses software to route the lines around farm drains and bird nests. It saves Rashid a day of arguing with maps. I think that's lovely.

S0.say: She'd say the robots aren't coming, so let's get on with it, and maybe post something cheeky about the money spent on hype.
S0.think: Privately she'd be slightly disappointed, because she likes gadgets and hoped her shoulders might get a break. But steady work to 66 is a good deal after thirty years of freelance uncertainty.
S0.do: Keeps going, qualifies in 2027 and keeps using the AI tools she already relies on, perhaps buying a better tablet for study. Changes nothing else.
S0.feel: Calm, with a small sigh of disappointment.
S0.quote: Freelancing taught us that the phone can stop ringing on a Tuesday. It also taught me not to panic when it does.
S0.fieldNote: Freya is the only one on her crew comfortable at height, thanks to theatre rigging, but struggles with heavy hauling and rule books. Thirty years of freelance work shaped how she handles uncertainty. She's slightly let down by a world without AI change, which is unusual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's use it to make the work safer and lighter. At work I'd be the one asking to try the new kit first. Online I'd probably share videos of whatever clever machine shows up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this suits me. My weak spots are muscle and memory for the rules, and that's exactly what machines and AI help with. A lifting robot and a talking rule book would make me as good as the young men.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ostwind to put me on any trial crew, starting this winter. I'd spend about 1,200 on a drone and get a licence, because grid inspection is going that way. And I'd keep studying for my ticket, because you have to know the job before you can tell a machine how to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious, if anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Pieter, who's been stringing wire for 35 years and won't touch a tablet. He's brilliant, but he'd hate this. I'd try to be his translator, the way I was for the old lighting men when everything went digital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd spend 1,200 on a drone. Isn't that risky with four months saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. But I've bought my own lights and ropes all my life. You invest in your tools or you're the one nobody calls. If the drone gets me one extra skill on the crew, it's paid for.

S1.say: She'd welcome using AI to make the work safer and lighter, ask to try new kit first and share videos of clever machines online.
S1.think: Privately she thinks this suits her, because her weaknesses are strength and remembering rules, exactly what machines and AI help with. A lifting robot and a talking rule book would level her with the young men.
S1.do: Asks to join any trial crew this winter, spends about 1,200 on a drone and gets a licence for grid inspection. Keeps studying for her qualification.
S1.quote: A lifting robot and a talking rule book would make me as good as the young men.
S1.fieldNote: Freya sees technology as a fix for her particular weaknesses as an older woman in a heavy trade. She's willing to put her own money into tools, a habit from freelancing. She offers to translate for an older colleague, as she did in theatre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast and the people in charge weren't ready, which isn't news. I'd say we have to make sure there's a person responsible for every robot near a live line. And I'd be curious, out loud, which probably wouldn't win me friends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means my job and Jonas's both get hit, because robots that build lines can build kitchens. I'd be 60. But I've lost my whole trade once already, in a few weeks, and I found another one. I know what it's like to start from nothing, and I'm not frightened of it the way some people are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right away, I'd ask Ostwind to make me one of the people who sets up and runs the robots, since I'm the one already using all this. I'd save hard, from four months to six if I can, and stop the holiday fund. And I'd look at going freelance again, offering robot setup to small solar farms, because that's the kind of work I know how to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's a big storm, but I've been out in storms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're not frightened. Is that the whole truth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not the whole truth. I'm frightened for Jonas, because he's not built for change like I am and his hands are his whole pride. For me, it's more like a knot in my stomach than real fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years of warning change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I wouldn't have time to qualify, so I'd go straight to the robot side and skip my ticket. Two years is enough to grab one skill, not build a new career. I'd grab the robot one.

S2.say: She'd say it came too fast for those in charge and insist on a responsible person for every robot near a live line. She'd voice curiosity openly, knowing it might not be popular.
S2.think: Privately she expects both her job and her carpenter husband's to be hit, and she'd be 60. But having already lost one trade in a few weeks and found another, she isn't frightened of starting again.
S2.do: Asks her employer to make her one of the people who set up and run the robots, saves hard from four months towards six and stops the holiday fund. Looks at going freelance again, offering robot setup to small solar farms.
S2.feel: Uneasy, with a knot in her stomach, but she's been out in storms before.
S2.quote: It's a big storm, but I've been out in storms.
S2.fieldNote: Freya's freelance past and her pandemic job loss make her unusually steady about a sudden shock. Her worry is for her husband's craft rather than for herself. With only two years she'd skip her qualification and go straight for robot skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to train people properly, and that companies like Ostwind should start training now. I'd volunteer to help design the training. Online I'd post about what I was learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is the sweet spot for me. I'd qualify, then train on the robots, and by 2031 I'd be a 63-year-old who knows both the line and the machine. That's rare, and rare gets paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my ticket in 2027, then do a robotics maintenance course at the technical college in the evenings from 2028. I'd keep the drone licence going. Jonas and I would look at him moving into restoring old furniture, the sort of thing people pay extra for because a person did it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Actually a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a moment you'd know it was really coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When I see a robot stringing wire between two poles without a crane operator. That's the hard bit in our work. Once I see that on a video from a real site, I'd stop worrying about my ticket and go all in on the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep looking for the upside. Is there a downside you're not saying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pension. I came into this at 55, so it's small whatever happens. If I get pushed out at 63 instead of 66, it's smaller still. That's the part I don't like to think about.

S3.say: She'd say five years is enough to train people properly and that companies should start now, offering to help design the training and posting about what she was learning.
S3.think: Privately she sees five years as her sweet spot: qualify, then train on robots, and be a rare 63-year-old who knows both the line and the machine.
S3.do: Gets her qualification in 2027, then studies robotics maintenance at evening classes from 2028 and keeps her drone licence. Helps her husband look at restoring old furniture, where human craft is valued.
S3.quote: That's rare, and rare gets paid.
S3.fieldNote: Freya treats five years as an opportunity and lays out a year-by-year plan. When pushed, she admits her small late-start pension is the downside she avoids thinking about. She has a clear signal for going all in: a robot stringing wire on a real site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's do this well. I'd tell anyone young on the crew to learn both the tools and the robots. I'd probably start a little online group for older women in the trades, about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it's fine. I'd retire at 66 in 2034, or keep going part-time if there's interesting robot work. I'd quite like to see it happen from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, qualify, learn the robots as they arrive rather than all at once. In the last few years before I retire, I might do a bit of freelance consulting on robot setup at small solar farms, to top up the pension. Jonas would carry on with his carpentry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Curious about the ending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a group for older women in the trades?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because there are about four of us in the whole region, and the training never thinks of us. If the robots arrive, I want us at the front of the queue for the new jobs, not shoved aside because we're 60 and female.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your kids about this decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Theo does sound for concerts, like I did lights. I'd tell him to learn the new systems now and keep his ears, because a good ear is hard to copy. Ines teaches small children, and I think she's the safest of all of us.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is time to do it well, urge young crew members to learn both the tools and the robots, and start an online group for older women in the trades.
S4.think: Privately she feels fine: she'd retire at 66 in 2034 or work part-time on interesting robot work, and she'd like to see the change from the inside.
S4.do: Keeps going, qualifies and learns the robots gradually. Plans some freelance consulting on robot setup at small solar farms before retiring to top up her pension.
S4.feel: Calm and curious about how it ends.
S4.quote: If the robots arrive, I want us at the front of the queue for the new jobs, not shoved aside because we're 60 and female.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Freya is relaxed and almost eager to see the change from inside. Her concern turns to the handful of older women in the trades, who she feels training schemes overlook. Freelance work keeps showing up as her natural fallback.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, mainly for Jonas. Carpentry is his whole identity, and he'd have no time to find a new shape for it. What would help is quick, cheap training on the new machines for people already in trades, and some income support for self-employed people like him, who fall through every gap.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they've already survived. I lost a thirty-year trade in about six weeks when the theatres shut. It's why I'm calmer than I probably should be. You learn that a career is something you carry in your hands, not something a company gives you.

headlineQuote: You learn that a career is something you carry in your hands, not something a company gives you.
portrait: Freya Ziegler is a 58-year-old second-year apprentice on Ostwind Energy's grid-connection crew, building lines from solar and wind farms across farmland, after thirty years rigging lights for concerts and theatres. She uses AI every day, is the only one on her crew happy at height, and struggles with heavy hauling and thick rule books. She's pragmatic in her politics and sees AI and robots as a fix for her own weak spots. Even AGI in two years leaves her only uneasy, because she has already lost a trade once and freelancing taught her to handle shocks, though she worries for her carpenter husband. With five or ten years she lays out a plan to become someone who knows both the line and the machine.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, mainly for her husband, a self-employed carpenter who would have no time to adapt.
whatWouldHelp: Quick, cheap training on new machines for people already in trades, and income support for self-employed workers who fall through the gaps.
